A 13-year-old girl from a hilly region of Nepal presented with intermittent fever with chills and profuse sweating for 1 month. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. There was no icterus, lymphadenopathy, cyanosis, clubbing, edema, or sternal tenderness. Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly extending to the umbilical line and mild hepatomegaly, with the liver palpable two fingers below the right midclavicular line. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.2 g/dL, total leukocyte count 3150/µL, and absolute neutrophil count 1386/µL. Blood glucose and electrolytes were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 46 mm/h, and C-reactive protein was reactive. Liver enzymes were elevated with ALT 130 U/L and AST 143 U/L. A chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed gross hepatosplenomegaly with a liver span of 16.2 cm and spleen span of 18.1 cm.

clinical_record:
A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. 

She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. 

Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. Because of the absence of pathological enhancement of the pons, this was felt to represent either an aggressive demyelinating process or a low-grade glioma. The patient continued to deteriorate, became comatose, and died approximately four weeks after admission.

A 25-year-old woman presented with a painless lump in the left cheek, first noted nine months earlier. She reported no toothache, numbness, or systemic symptoms and had no significant medical history. On examination, there was left facial asymmetry without skin changes. An orthopantomogram showed no bony destruction of the mandible or maxilla, with only a healed post-extraction socket in the region of tooth 36. Ultrasonography of the left cheek demonstrated a discrete, well-demarcated, hypoechoic solid mass measuring 2.6 × 2.0 cm, overlying the parotid gland, with no increase in internal vascular flow or calcification. Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and neck revealed a well-bordered, slightly enhancing soft-tissue tumor measuring 2.7 × 3.7 × 4.0 cm in the left buccal space, indenting but not destroying adjacent bones (including the posterior maxillary sinus wall, medial pterygoid, masseter, and temporal muscle), and extending into the temporal space; the mass was supplied by branches of the left buccal artery.

Fine-needle aspiration biopsy yielded a hypocellular sample with erythrocytes, histiocytes, and neutrophils but showed “no signs of malignancy.” An intraoral incisional biopsy demonstrated “wide fibroblast proliferation, extremely similar to a fibroma.”

An 8‐year‐old boy with no significant past medical history presented with a 30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain followed by a single episode of vomiting. During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. The episode lasted 10 minutes, after which he reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea. Family denied toxin or medication exposure. He had a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate, and he was performing well in school.

On admission, his vital signs were normal except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation; he could not recognize his mother or speak but could follow visual commands. Motor and sensory examinations were normal.
